title: Father, 40, 2 Kids Has $3M Invested, Gets Laid Off — ‘I Think I’m Done!’
detail:
Father, 40, 2 Kids Has $3M Invested, Gets Laid Off — ‘I Think I’m Done!’
Image via Shutterstock
Casey B. Renner
Sun, September 27, 2026 at 10:00 AM CDT 7 min read
RDDT

A 40-year-old father of two thought he still had more time before deciding whether to walk away from his career. Then he found out his employer was letting him go.

But with $3 million invested and his wife planning to keep working, he isn't looking for another job.

"I think I'm done!" he wrote on Reddit.

Don't Miss:

Warren Buffett once said, "If you don't find a way to make money while you sleep, you will work until you die." Here's how you can earn passive income with just $100.

Forget The Rental Property. Some Investors Are Using Real Estate Notes Instead.

He Had $3 Million Invested And Still Planned To Work Longer

The poster had considered quitting eight months earlier but decided to work for at least another 18 months. At the time, they thought another three years on the job could put them in an even stronger position.

The poster's wife already had about $3 million invested in diversified stock exchange-traded funds, including roughly $700,000 in their 401(k)s. They had built most of their wealth through careers in law and tax advisory.

With the poster's wife planning to work for at least another three years, they don't need to start living off that money yet because her income covers their expenses.

"So basically I'm coast [financial independence, retire early]/ stay at home dad for now," they wrote.

Staying Home Means Taking On A Different Kind Of Work

The poster wants more time with their kids while they're young and more freedom to ski, mountain bike and occasionally take a midweek trip.

Trending: AI Needs More Power Than The Grid Can Easily Provide. This Startup Is Taking A Different Approach To Energy Storage.

Someone who had been in a similar position suggested making home responsibilities part of their new routine. "Treat home stuff like a job," the person wrote, adding that they should "make sure she still gets time for her own activities."

There was also the day-to-day work of having two young children at home. "Might I suggest taking on the vast majority of household tasks like cooking, cleaning, groceries," one person wrote. "I have two kids under 4 years old and taking care of them is a full time job in itself…"

The $160,000 Question Comes Once They're Both Retired

Once they're both retired, the couple expects to spend about $160,000 a year, including taxes and health care. The original poster hopes their investments will be closer to $4 million by then and is comfortable starting with a withdrawal rate of about 5%.

Reddit shares have dropped sharply year to date, and with the stock back under pressure, the live question is whether today's valuation can be squared with the earnings power the business is putting on the table.

The stock is down 38.1% year to date, which puts the focus firmly on whether the current share price still lines up with what Reddit earns.

Recent revenue growth and user trends suggest the platform may support higher profitability over time, which feeds directly into how investors frame its earnings base.

There is a second opinion on Reddit worth weighing. See what analysts think Reddit's shares could be worth.

The stock's next move may depend on whether Reddit's current price is justified by its earnings today and the profit stream investors expect to see from here.

If you are weighing Reddit against other opportunities tied to earnings power, it can help to compare it with 32 high quality undervalued stocks.

Has Reddit Run Too Far on Earnings?

A P/E lens fits Reddit because the market is clearly keying off earnings power and the recent profit narrative. On this metric, the stock trades at about 33.1x earnings, which is above both the Interactive Media and Services sector average of roughly 10.1x and a peer group mark near 28.8x. That is a meaningfully richer tag than the broad industry and also a premium to closer comparables.

The Fair Ratio model, which adjusts for Reddit's growth profile, margins, size and risk, points to a lower P/E than where the shares change hands today, so the current multiple screens as overvalued on this framework. Because the latest Q2 report showed strong revenue and user metrics, the high P/E appears to reflect confidence that these fundamentals can sustain Reddit's earnings story. title: Reddit Stock Is Down Nearly 35% in 2026, Yet Wall Street Sees Revenue Topping $5 Billion by 2028

Reddit Stock Is Down Nearly 35% in 2026, Yet Wall Street Sees Revenue Topping $5 Billion by 2028
Wiltone Asuncion
Sat, September 26, 2026 at 8:14 AM CDT 4 min read
RDDT
Trade Reddit on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Reddit Stock Is Down Nearly 35% in 2026, Yet Wall Street Sees Revenue Topping $5 Billion by 2028 ©@Brett Jordan from Pexels via Canva, @Karola G from Pexels via Canva
Key Stats for Reddit Stock

Current Price: $149.84

Target Price (Mid): ~$305

Street Target: ~$214

Potential Total Return: ~104%

Annualized IRR: ~18% / year

What Happened?

Reddit (RDDT) closed at $149.84 on September 25, down 34.8% from the end of 2025. Over the same stretch, TIKR consensus for 2028 revenue rose from around $4.8 billion to around $5.5 billion. That's past the range investors fear Reddit will stall in.

CEO Steve Huffman addressed that range at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference on September 8, listing it among the misconceptions he hears: "I think investors worry that Reddit is going to get stuck at the $4 billion to $5 billion revenue range because some of our similarly scaled peers have gotten stuck there."

Huffman's Case Rests on Reach and Commerce

Huffman's case against the ceiling is reach and commerce: "our TAM is literally everybody," he said, and "40% of the conversations on Reddit are commercial."

Reddit has topped the high end of its own revenue guidance in each of the last five quarters, by 11% in Q2. Its Q3 guide of $860 million to $870 million implies growth of about 48% at the midpoint, down from 61% in Q2. The average estimate of around $872 million sits just above the top of that range.

Reddit Revenue & EBITDA (TIKR)
U.S. Users Explain Why Reddit Trades Below Meta

U.S. daily active uniques slipped to 53.2 million in Q2 from 53.5 million in Q1 as search referrals turned choppy. On July 30, Huffman said Google's AI Overviews can't replace traditional search links for traffic.

U.S. logged-in users grew just 1% year over year. U.S. revenue still grew 56%, as revenue per U.S. daily user rose 51% to $11.85. International daily users rose 28% to 77.1 million, with $2.26 in revenue each.

Shares fell 20.99% the session after the report. Reddit will also stop disclosing the logged-in split starting with Q3.

Huffman argued that traffic "that's logged out or transient is just less meaningful to us, which is why we can see volatility in SEO traffic, and that doesn't turn into volatility in our business."

Reddit's NTM P/E ratio of around 18x sits below Meta Platforms' at around 23x and Alphabet's at around 26x. The discount disappears on NTMEV/EBITDA, where Reddit's around 15x tops Meta's around 12x. The P/E flatters Reddit: its 2026 normalized EPS estimate of around $7.70 runs well above the GAAP estimate of around $5.40.

Reddit NTM Price / Normalized Earnings (P/E) (TIKR)

Reddit's content deals with Google and OpenAI reportedly expire next year. Huffman declined to discuss the Google talks in detail because Reddit is "in active negotiation." Other revenue, including licensing, was 5.3% of Q2 sales.

title: Reddit (RDDT) vs Snap (SNAP): Which is a Better Stock to Buy?
detail:
Reddit (RDDT) vs Snap (SNAP): Which is a Better Stock to Buy?
Suraj Santlani
Fri, September 25, 2026 at 10:28 PM CDT 4 min read
SNAP
RDDT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Reddit, Inc. (NYSE:RDDT) and Snap Inc. (NYSE:SNAP) are both selling advertising against an audience that did not exist twenty years ago, and both have been punished this year. Reddit is down roughly a third, Snap about the same.

That is where the symmetry ends. Snap collects far more revenue and loses money. Reddit collects far less and earns a profit margin above 30%.

READ ALSO: Jim Cramer Is Holding Back on Snap (SNAP) Until It Shows a Profit

Reddit (RDDT) vs Snap (SNAP): Which is a Better Stock to Buy?
Reddit Makes More From Fewer Users Than Snap Does:

Snap's revenue is roughly $6.35 billion a year against Reddit's $2.78 billion. On that basis, Snap looks like the larger business, and it is.

But Reddit grew about 67% over the past year while Snap grew about 13%, and Reddit turned its revenue into roughly $871 million of profit while Snap lost money. Snap's most recent quarter of revenue growth was better, closer to 19%, so the gap is narrowing from a very wide starting point.

The advertising gap explains most of it. On Reddit's own disclosure, its revenue per user in the United States now runs ahead of Snapchat's North American figure, though the two companies count users differently. Advertisers appear to like a place where people arrive asking for recommendations.

Reddit also has a revenue line Snap does not. It licenses its archive of human conversation to AI companies, with deals reported at roughly $60 million a year from Google. That is money from a market that did not exist two years ago, though the Google arrangement has been reported as at risk of renegotiation.

DON'T MISS: Reddit (RDDT) May Walk Away From Google's (GOOGL) $60 Million-a-Year Deal as AI Search Eats Its Traffic

Snap is a Third of the Price for a Reason:

Snap trades near eight times what analysts expect it to earn next year. Reddit trades near twenty-three times. Cheap is not the same as wrong.

Snap holds about $2.66 billion of cash, has a global audience that dwarfs Reddit's, and is not going out of business. If it simply stops losing money, the shares do not need much growth to work from here.

The problem is that it has been about to stop losing money for a long time. Snap has spent years launching products, most recently a set of smart glasses, while the core advertising business fails to convert scale into profit.

Reddit carries its own risk, and it is the reverse. It depends on search traffic that AI assistants are increasingly intercepting, answering questions without sending anyone to the site. The licensing money that looks like a new revenue stream partly compensates for the traffic those same companies are taking away.
